outputs.L2:
Give the plants a drink. Hydrate yourself generously. Avoid listening to current events. Let boredom happen. Grumble about the climate. Carry a wine opener in your handbag. Occasionally swipe to the right. Smile only when you genuinely feel like it. Stay in bed late. Keep the news out of sight. Bear in mind how white people experience the world. Hear the crickets sing. Clean between your teeth. Take your medication. Leave your thoughts blank.

If you wake with a hangover, never swear that you will quit drinking forever. Tell the truth when you have the strength. When you do not, hydrate, deceive yourself, switch off the broadcasts, set the newspapers alight, miss the memorial services, swallow your pills, laugh at stupid nonsense, sleep with people who mean nothing to you, and make use of the slow cooker, the juicer, and the blender. Drink what falls from the clouds. Do not dwell on the heavens, and do not contemplate water. Stay away from the funerals. Shut your eyes at every opportunity.

While raising a glass, meet each person’s gaze. Do not place punctuation around the President. Create the news yourself. Become liquid. Pour water over the fire escape. Incinerate the page. Crush the correspondence. Choose hydrangeas rather than hyacinths. Give the hydrangeas water. Make the news wither. Turn the hydrangeas white. Drink the whiteness. Transform the crickets’ music into a cascade. Let your mind hold a melody. Withhold your smile. Do not fade—funeral, funeral.
outputs.L3:
Begin with the basics of self-care. Drink enough water, get the sleep you need, floss your teeth, take prescribed medication as directed, and tend to the plants or other small responsibilities that depend on you. These ordinary acts may seem insignificant, but they create stability when everything else feels uncertain.

Protect yourself from unnecessary distress. Turn off relentless news broadcasts, discard papers that only deepen your anxiety, and resist the urge to analyze every event or emotion. You do not need to remain informed, reflective, or productive at every moment. Sometimes it is enough to quiet your mind and let the day pass without demanding that it provide answers.

Make room for boredom and uncomplicated pleasure. Step outside, listen to music, laugh when something genuinely amuses you, and take comfort in familiar household rituals. Water the plants, wash a cup, open a window, or watch the light move across a room. Small acts of attention can offer moments of escape without requiring you to leave your life behind.

Allow yourself to be imperfect. You may complain, indulge, avoid difficult truths, or seek casual intimacy without pretending it means more than it does. Do not make grand promises simply to make a fleeting moment feel permanent. At the same time, treat yourself and others with care: respect consent, communicate clearly, and avoid choices that place anyone’s health or safety at risk.

Above all, preserve your boundaries and remain as authentic as you can. Smile only when you genuinely want to. Be honest when you have the strength, and refrain from needless deception when you do not. When you raise a glass with others, meet their eyes. Even in small gestures, let your presence be sincere and your choices remain your own.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts the experience of political and emotional overwhelm by placing large public crises alongside the small routines of ordinary life. Rather than offering a single argument or a clear solution, it unfolds as a stream of instructions: attend to the home, care for the body, step away from the news, perform manageable tasks, and find temporary forms of relief. These commands suggest a speaker trying to remain functional while surrounded by grief, anxiety, and relentless information. Domestic advice and self-care rituals become practical responses to forces that otherwise feel too immense to confront.

Yet the poem does not present coping as simple or entirely successful. Its gestures of avoidance and distraction provide shelter, but only briefly. The news continues to intrude, and references to water and funerals keep returning the poem to ideas of danger, mourning, and loss. Water is especially unstable as an image: it can cleanse and sustain, but it can also flood, overwhelm, or carry things away. In this way, the poem’s imagery reflects the speaker’s emotional state, moving between the desire for renewal and the fear of being submerged.

As the language becomes more surreal, wordplay offers another form of survival. Familiar meanings loosen, unexpected associations emerge, and painful realities are imaginatively rearranged. This verbal transformation does not erase political violence or private grief, but it creates a space in which they can be approached indirectly. Humor, absurdity, and linguistic play function both as evasions and as acts of resistance, preventing the language of crisis from completely determining the speaker’s inner life.

The repeated commands give the poem urgency while also exposing uncertainty. They sound like advice, but their accumulation suggests that no single instruction is enough. The speaker must keep generating new rituals, diversions, and ways of thinking because each coping mechanism is temporary and incomplete. Survival therefore appears not as a state of mastery, but as an ongoing practice made up of imperfect acts of care, distraction, resistance, and imaginative transformation. The poem ultimately reveals both the necessity and the fragility of these acts: they cannot resolve the crises that produce fear and grief, but they may make it possible to continue living through them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse prose poem made of contradictory self-care instructions, political avoidance, drinking advice, household objects, flowers, water, news, and funerals. Let the language gradually unravel and abandon punctuation near the end.
counterfactuals.output:
Begin the morning by forgiving yourself  
for everything you will refuse to forgive.

Drink eight glasses of water,  
unless the water remembers the election.  
In that case, pour it into the fern  
and apologize to the roots for bringing up government.

Breathe deeply, but not so deeply  
that the country enters your lungs.  
Keep the news folded beneath the toaster,  
where its small wars can warm the crumbs.  
Do not read the headlines before breakfast.  
Do not eat breakfast until you know  
which cities have vanished.

For clarity, drink nothing stronger than moonlight.  
For courage, add two fingers of whiskey.  
For sleep, place the glass beside the bed  
and let it drink you.

Polish the spoons.  
They have reflected too many mouths.  
Turn every chair toward the wall  
so no one has to take a position.  
If asked what you believe,  
say chrysanthemums.  
If pressed, say rain.  
If pressed harder, become a locked cupboard  
full of clean towels and thunder.

Attend your own funeral once a week.  
Wear something bright.  
Arrive late, carrying lilies  
that insist they are sirens.  
Stand beside the coffin and whisper:  
You look rested.  
Then go home and overwork yourself gently.

Hydrate. Dehydrate.  
Take a bath in yesterday’s news.  
Do not let the ink touch your conscience.  
Rinse with cold water  
until every border closes.

Call your mother, unless she is dead.  
If she is dead, call anyway.  
Let the telephone ring in the soil.  
Someone beneath the marigolds  
may need to hear a familiar weather.

Avoid political discussion at dinner.  
Serve the ballot box as a centerpiece.  
Fill it with peonies, forks, and unopened envelopes.  
When the guests ask who you voted for,  
raise your glass and toast the ceiling fan,  
which spins equally for everyone  
and goes nowhere.

Remember moderation.  
Have one drink for the living,  
one for the dead,  
one for the person you were  
before the broadcast interrupted the rain.  
Pour the fourth into the sink.  
Watch the drain accept responsibility.

Before bed, unplug the lamp  
so darkness may conserve energy.  
Tuck the kettle under a blanket.  
Tell the mirror it is beautiful  
but should stop spreading rumors.

Tomorrow wake early and remain asleep  
wash your hands in dust  
keep calm until calm becomes a riot  
feed the roses salt  
give the ocean a glass of water  
do not look at the news it is looking at you

carry the coffin into the kitchen  
set it beside the blue cup the bent key the patient knife  
ask no questions answer all flowers

the lilies say drink  
the water says burn  
the radio opens its black mouth  
and every name falls out wet

we fold the names into towels  
we fold the towels into flags  
we fold the flags into boats  
we fold the boats into mouths

no more weather no more whether  
no more vote only violet  
only glass only grass only grief learning to breathe

and breathe don’t breathe  
sleep wake swallow the river  
the house is full of rainchairs  
the table has elected a wound  
the spoons are singing funeral funeral fern

water the dead  
bury the news  
drink the door  
close the flower

be well be unwell be welling  
be the bell the bowl the blue below

and when morning comes without coming  
hold yourself apart together  
softly loudly  
alive not alive

al  
li  
water  
ward  
flower  
fall  
all
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem in the form of a chaotic list of life advice for surviving modern America, mixing mundane habits with dark humor, privilege, sex, grief, and anxiety about the news.
counterfactuals.output:
**HOW TO REMAIN A PERSON, PROBABLY**

1. Drink water. The empire prefers you dehydrated and clicking.

2. Call your mother, if possible.  
   If not possible, call the silence where she used to answer.  
   Let it ring.

3. Learn one cheap recipe involving beans. Learn another involving denial.

4. When the news says *breaking,* check whether anything inside you has already broken.  
   Apply pressure.  
   Do not refresh.

5. Keep cash in a jar marked **DENTIST / ESCAPE / SEX MOTEL.**

6. Floss. Civilization is mostly maintenance performed while tired.

7. If you are white, notice when the room becomes easy for you.  
   Do not call this ease “neutral.”  
   Do not ask for a medal because you noticed.

8. Have sex with the lights on, off, or flickering like a federal agency.  
   Ask what feels good.  
   Believe the answer.  
   Stop if the answer changes.

9. Purchase fewer storage bins. You are not organizing your life;  
   you are building little plastic mausoleums for charging cables.

10. Vote, yes, but do not confuse voting with innocence.

11. Keep a coat by the door.  
    Keep shoes you can run in.  
    Hate that this sounds practical.

12. Never read the comments after midnight.  
    At midnight, every stranger becomes a senator in the republic of your cortisol.

13. Tip well. Someone is carrying eight waters and a private emergency.

14. If you inherit money, inherit the haunting too.

15. Say: *I don’t know.*  
    Say: *I was wrong.*  
    Say: *The rent is obscene.*  
    Say the name of the dead person, even if everyone’s face becomes weather.

16. Buy the generic medication.  
    Buy the expensive sunscreen.  
    Steal nothing except time from your employer.

17. Your phone is not a window.  
    It is a slot machine filled with funerals.

18. Touch grass, as instructed.  
    Check for ticks, as required by the nation.

19. Make friends with someone who owns a drill, someone who knows CPR,  
    someone who will tell you when you are being unbearable.

20. Become that last person for somebody else.

21. Do not monetize your healing.  
    Not every wound needs a newsletter.

22. The supermarket has seventeen kinds of mustard  
    and one exhausted cashier.  
    This is called freedom by people who have never needed insulin.

23. Masturbate before sending the text.  
    Sleep before sending the email.  
    Consult a lawyer before sending the manifesto.

24. Plant something native.  
    Apologize when it dies.  
    Plant again.

25. Grief is not a lesson.  
    Grief is a dog that eats the lesson and waits beside your bed.

26. If the headline contains the phrase **THIS CHANGES EVERYTHING,**  
    finish your sandwich first.

27. Keep your passport current if you have one.  
    Know that having one is already a kind of door.

28. Dance badly at the wedding.  
    Cry discreetly in the pharmacy.  
    Laugh at the funeral only when the dead would have laughed harder.

29. Learn which neighbors have generators  
    and which neighbors have no one.

30. In the active-shooter training, note the exits.  
    In the elementary school, note the tiny backpacks.  
    Go home and make dinner somehow.

31. Cancel subscriptions before they become beliefs.

32. Forgive yourself selectively.  
    Some guilt is a smoke alarm.  
    Some guilt just needs a new battery.

33. Do not date anyone who says they are “brutally honest.”  
    They are usually more interested in the brutality.

34. Stretch your hips. Fascism loves a stiff electorate.

35. If you can afford therapy, go.  
    If you cannot, reject the idea that suffering is your budgeting error.

36. Keep joy in unmarked containers.

37. Remember: the algorithm is not worried about you.  
    It is worried you might look away.

38. Look away.

39. Look back when someone needs a witness.

40. Survive without making survival your only god.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness “how to live” manifesto from the perspective of a hungover, politically exhausted woman. Use repeated imperatives such as “drink water,” “don’t smile,” and “skip the funerals,” ending in dreamlike wordplay.
counterfactuals.output:
Drink water. Drink water before coffee, after coffee, instead of calling him, instead of reading the news, because the news has learned to crawl beneath the door and sleep at the foot of the bed. Don’t smile when they tell you to. Don’t smile for the photograph, the meeting, the man explaining fire to the woman already burning. Keep your face like a locked apartment.

Open a window. Close the app. Salt the eggs. Take the pills with food. Vote, if only to leave a small bruise on the machine. Then go home. Take off the bra, the boots, the century. Don’t argue after midnight. Don’t explain your anger to people who collect explanations like trophies. Drink water.

Skip the funerals. Not all of them—just the funerals for parties, promises, respectable men, the idea that history bends without being shoved. Send flowers if you must. Send thorns. Stay in bed and mourn privately, with one eye open and the television muttering about markets, missiles, weather. Let the dead bury the headlines.

Call your mother. Don’t call your mother. Write it down and decide tomorrow. Feed the cat. Feed yourself. Eat something green enough to remember rain. Don’t smile. Stretch your back. Unclench the fist you have mistaken for a heart.

Believe nobody before breakfast. Believe everybody a little after soup. Carry cash. Carry aspirin. Carry one impossible hope in the torn lining of your coat. Skip the funerals. Attend the births, especially your own, which happens whenever you stop apologizing.

Drink water. Drink the dark between words. Wake slowly. Walk softly into the loud republic of morning, where the sun is a pun with no punchline, where ballots become ballads, where mourning misplaces its *u* and turns to morning, and every broken promise opens its mouth and out flies a small blue maybe, maybe-bird, may-be, be-may, winging west through the whiskey-colored weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an absurdist prose poem that begins with recognizable wellness tips but progressively becomes fragmented and nonsensical? Include a corkscrew, dating apps, cricket songs, hydrangeas, the President, and recurring images of water and newspapers.
counterfactuals.output:
Drink eight glasses of water a day. Stretch when you wake. Eat something green, breathe deeply, limit your time on dating apps, and take a brisk walk beneath the hydrangeas. Sleep for eight hours, if possible. Read the newspaper only after breakfast, so the headlines do not enter the empty rooms of your body.

At noon, drink more water. The body is mostly water and therefore mostly weather. Stand straight. Roll your shoulders back. Unclench the small blue fist behind your forehead.

If you feel lonely, open a window. Listen to the cricket songs sawing the dusk into useful portions. Do not compare your life to anyone else’s carefully illuminated picnic. The corkscrew also spirals downward before the bottle opens.

By evening, the dating apps begin ringing underwater. A man named Tuesday is holding a trout in every photograph. A woman made entirely of newspapers asks whether you enjoy travel. You say yes, although your shoes have filled with rain and the President is asleep in the hydrangeas, dreaming of a larger President.

Remember to hydrate.

Remember to hydrate the newspaper.

Fold a glass of water into quarters and place it beneath your tongue. The headlines will soften. The corkscrew will announce tomorrow’s pollen count. Crickets, having misplaced their songs, hum the passwords to abandoned accounts:

bluehorse, bluehorse, acceptable moon.

Swipe left on the moon. Swipe right on the staircase. Match with a bucket that lives three miles away and “isn’t looking for anything serious.” The bucket sends water. The water sends newspapers. The newspapers are damp with the President’s fingerprints, though the President now denies having fingers.

Breathe in for four hydrangeas.

Hold for seven corkscrews.

Exhale until the crickets become furniture.

Now the body is ninety percent newspaper, ten percent please. Water the please. Date the water. Unscrew the horizon. In the kitchen, a headline swims laps around an empty glass:

PRESIDENT MARRIES THURSDAY  
CRICKETS DECLARE INDOOR WEATHER  
HYDRANGEAS FOUND GUILTY OF BLUE

You should get eight hours of blue each night.

You should walk briskly through the bottle.

You should not—  
the water—  
newspaper ankles, corkscrew noon—  
the President refreshing, refreshing—  
all the little cricket apps singing yes no yes no wet—

Hydrangea, hydrangea, open the door.

There is no door.

Only water reading water  
and the newspaper folding itself smaller  
smaller  
into a cup  
into a mouth  
into—

drink.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a punctuation-light collage poem built from commands and prohibitions. Contrast domestic appliances and self-care routines with racial awareness, media fatigue, death, alcohol, and surreal transformations into water, fire, flowers, and song.
counterfactuals.output:
unplug the toaster  
do not unplug your history  

wash your face in cold headlines  
rinse until the anchors stop shouting  
do not mistake silence for safety  

load the dishwasher  
count the knives  
remember who is watched in the grocery aisle  
remember who is followed home  

moisturize your hands  
do not soften the truth  
name the color line  
name the names they shorten on television  

turn off the screen  
let the breaking news break without you  
do not drink the whole bottle  
pour one glass for the living  
pour one for the dead  

empty the lint trap  
empty your pockets of excuses  
do not call exhaustion peace  

brush your teeth  
scrub smoke from your tongue  
become water when the door is locked  
become fire when the room denies you air  

fold the towels  
unfold the sirens  
do not look away  
do not make a spectacle of looking  

set the timer  
cancel the timer  
death keeps its own kitchen  

water the flowers  
become the flowers  
rise bright from the mouths of the buried  

lower the volume  
open the window  
turn every warning into weather  
turn every wound into a chorus  

do not burn the house  
be the flame that finds the cold  
do not drown  
be the river that remembers every name  

sleep if you can  
wake if you must
